title: ABAIR's Irish synthetic voices power an NVDA screenreader plugin for visually impaired pupils, “extensively tested with visually-impaired school children”
summary: Trinity College Dublin's ABAIR team reports that its Irish synthetic voices power an NVDA screenreader plugin with Braille output, tested with visually impaired pupils; no outcome is reported.
account: Ní Chasaide, Barnes, Ní Chiaráin, McGuirk, Morrin, Nic Corcráin and Cummins of the ABAIR initiative described three assistive applications of ABAIR's Irish speech technology on 27 May 2022. They presented the paper at the Ninth Workshop on Speech and Language Processing for Assistive Technologies (SLPAT-2022). The first is “A screenreading facility for Irish has been developed as a plugin for the NVDA screenreader, prompted by urgent pleas from parents and grandparents of visually impaired children in the Gaeltacht or attending Irish-medium schools”. Only three books existed in Irish Braille for them. “With funding from the National Council for the Blind in Ireland (NCBI) a blind researcher worked with the ABAIR team to develop the NVDA screenreader plugin”. The plugin adds Braille output through the Liblouis translator. It lets users choose a male or female voice and the reading speed. The paper states: “The system was extensively tested with visually-impaired school children and a full technical description is available in McGuirk (2005)”. The reference list has McGuirk 2015, an M.Phil. dissertation. The paper names no child, school, date or measured result. It describes the voices as text-to-speech synthesis without stating the synthesis method. ABAIR staff wrote in a paper presented at SIGUL 2023, a meeting on under-resourced languages in Dublin (18 to 20 August 2023), that the project's accessibility applications include a downloadable screen-reading facility for the visually impaired. The Irish Braille tables in the Liblouis translator credit Ronan McGuirk (2019) and the Irish National Braille and Alternative Formats Authority (INBAF), which issued an updated version in 2025. ABAIR's screen reader page, which carries a 2026 copyright line, explains how to set up NVDA for Irish Braille output and says that users can also have the text read aloud. No cited source is independent of the developers.
purpose: Built so that blind and visually impaired pupils can hear and read Irish text through a screenreader with Braille output. Use by school children was that intended purpose.
system: ABAIR Irish-language synthetic voices (abair.ie) delivered through an NVDA screenreader plugin with Liblouis Braille output

deployer: Visually impaired pupils in Gaeltacht and Irish-medium schools, per the paper

ai_role.statement: The evidence is limited to the developers' account. The ABAIR team's SLPAT 2022 paper says the Irish NVDA plugin with their synthetic voices was built with a blind researcher. It was extensively tested with visually impaired school children, without any outcome data. The paper does not describe the synthesis method. So neither the system's AI character nor its contribution to any pupil's reading can be assessed from cited sources.

fields.summary: Trinity College Dublin's ABAIR team reports that its Irish synthetic voices power an NVDA screenreader plugin with Braille output, tested with visually impaired pupils; no outcome is reported.
fields.account: Ní Chasaide, Barnes, Ní Chiaráin, McGuirk, Morrin, Nic Corcráin and Cummins of the ABAIR initiative described three assistive applications of ABAIR's Irish speech technology on 27 May 2022. They presented the paper at the Ninth Workshop on Speech and Language Processing for Assistive Technologies (SLPAT-2022). The first is “A screenreading facility for Irish has been developed as a plugin for the NVDA screenreader, prompted by urgent pleas from parents and grandparents of visually impaired children in the Gaeltacht or attending Irish-medium schools”. Only three books existed in Irish Braille for them. “With funding from the National Council for the Blind in Ireland (NCBI) a blind researcher worked with the ABAIR team to develop the NVDA screenreader plugin”. The plugin adds Braille output through the Liblouis translator. It lets users choose a male or female voice and the reading speed. The paper states: “The system was extensively tested with visually-impaired school children and a full technical description is available in McGuirk (2005)”. The reference list has McGuirk 2015, an M.Phil. dissertation. The paper names no child, school, date or measured result. It describes the voices as text-to-speech synthesis without stating the synthesis method. ABAIR staff wrote in a paper presented at SIGUL 2023, a meeting on under-resourced languages in Dublin (18 to 20 August 2023), that the project's accessibility applications include a downloadable screen-reading facility for the visually impaired. The Irish Braille tables in the Liblouis translator credit Ronan McGuirk (2019) and the Irish National Braille and Alternative Formats Authority (INBAF), which issued an updated version in 2025. ABAIR's screen reader page, which carries a 2026 copyright line, explains how to set up NVDA for Irish Braille output and says that users can also have the text read aloud. No cited source is independent of the developers.
